record.original_question: An uphill lattice path is a doubly infinite monotone path in R^2 made of unit steps from (a, b) to either (a, b + 1) or (a + 1, b), and a downhill lattice path is defined similarly with b - 1 in place of b + 1. For a finite set P of points in Z^2, call such a monotone lattice path friendly if the number of points of P on one side of the path equals the number on the other side, ignoring points that lie on the path itself. Is it true that every odd-sized finite set of lattice points has a friendly path?

evidence.quote: An uphill lattice path is the union of a (doubly infinite) sequence of directed line segments in R^2, each connecting an integer pair (a, b) to an adjacent pair either (a, b + 1), (a + 1, b). A downhill lattice path is defined similarly, but with b - 1 in place of b + 1, and a monotone lattice path is an uphill or downhill lattice path. Given a finite set P of points in Z, a friendly path is a monotone lattice path for which there are as many points in P on one side of the path as on the other. (Points that lie on the path do not count.)
Problem 8. Is it true that for every odd-sized set of points there is a friendly path?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define an uphill lattice path in $\mathbb{R}^2$ to be the union of a doubly infinite sequence of unit directed line segments, each going from some integer point $(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ to either $(a,b+1)$ or $(a+1,b)$. Define a downhill lattice path in the same way, but with steps from $(a,b)$ to either $(a,b-1)$ or $(a+1,b)$. A monotone lattice path is an uphill or downhill lattice path. Such a path divides $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus(\text{path})$ into two open connected components ("sides"). 

Given a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$, a monotone lattice path is called friendly for $P$ if the number of points of $P$ lying strictly on one side of the path equals the number of points of $P$ strictly on the other side (points of $P$ that lie on the path are not counted on either side).

Question: Is it true that for every finite set $P\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$ of odd cardinality, there exists a friendly monotone lattice path?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is answered in the negative. Alkauskas (arXiv:2302.01137, "Friendly paths for finite subsets of plane integer lattice. I") exhibits inseparable odd-sized configurations: for odd $n\le 41$, the unique inseparable set (up to symmetry) has $n=27$, and further odd inseparable sizes such as $n=43,45$ also occur. Hence not every odd-sized finite set has a friendly monotone lattice path.

status_evidence.title: Friendly paths for finite subsets of plane integer lattice. I
status_evidence.snippet: If n is an odd number with n ≤ 41, and a set of n lattice points is inseparable, then n = 27. Up to G-symmetry, the configuration is unique.
status_evidence.claim: There exists an odd-sized (n=27) finite lattice point set with no friendly monotone lattice path, refuting the conjecture.

status_evidence.title: Friendly paths (full version) — G. Alkauskas
status_evidence.snippet: n = 27 and n = 43 are the first odd numbers with c(n) = 1, while n = 45 is the first odd with c(n) = 2.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple odd cardinalities admit inseparable point sets, so not every odd-sized set has a friendly path.
